title: Sands of the Ganges (section 11)
hook: as many rivers as the Ganges' sands, and worlds of treasure for each: still less than this teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mind that rests on nothing, the line tradition says woke Huineng. Your line: resting on nothing. When did a worry land and lift off again? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

Scoop a handful of sand from a riverbank and try counting the grains. The count slips long before the hand is empty. Now the Diamond Sutra asks for something stranger. Take the river Ganges, and count its sand. Then, for every single grain, add another whole Ganges. Now count the sand in all of those rivers. The mind gives up somewhere around the second step, and that's the point. When this sutra wants a number too big for numbers, it reaches for river sand. Today: sands of the Ganges.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF SAND.` → `A GANGES FOR EVERY GRAIN.` → `A NUMBER TOO BIG FOR NUMBERS.`

segments.voice: First, the rivers. The Buddha asks Subhuti: if there were as many rivers Ganges as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, would the sand in all those rivers be much? Very much, Subhuti says. The rivers alone would be beyond counting, let alone their sand. Second, the treasure. Now, the Buddha says, suppose a good man or a good woman filled as many worlds as there are grains in all those rivers with precious things, and gave it all away. Would the merit be great? Very great, Subhuti says. Notice the sutra's words, a good man or a good woman. Both are named, here and elsewhere in this sutra. Third, the turn. Yet if a good man or a good woman keeps even four lines of this sutra and explains them to others, the Buddha says, that merit is greater. Fourth, why say it twice? Section eight already set four lines against a world system of treasure. Here the scale on the other side is made unimaginably larger, and the answer doesn't move. That's how this sutra teaches. It doesn't add a new argument. It turns the volume up on the same one until the size of the pile stops mattering. Because that's the real lesson inside the arithmetic. The treasure side keeps growing, and it's still the wrong kind of thing. Grains can be counted, at least in principle. Gifts can be counted. What a few lines of understanding do in a person, when they're passed on at the right moment, isn't on that scale at all. Two piles, then: one that can be counted, and one that can't.
screen: `A GANGES FOR EVERY GRAIN.` · `WORLDS OF TREASURE GIVEN AWAY.` · `STILL LESS THAN FOUR LINES.` · `THE VOLUME TURNED UP.` · then, large: `MORE THAN THE SAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: count one blessing. Just one. Settle, and breathe. The sutra has just spent a whole section on numbers too big to hold, so go the other way. Let one good thing in your life come to mind. A person, a meal, a morning, a few words that once helped. Don't add a second. Don't rank it. Just hold the one, and let it be enough, the way four lines were enough. If the list starts to grow, smile at it, and come back to the one. The bell holds the time.
Sands of the Ganges. As many rivers as the Ganges has grains, worlds of treasure for each grain, and still four lines passed on are worth more. Today's word.
Your line: more than the sand. Today, when you catch yourself counting, money, likes, tasks, notice one thing in the day that won't fit on that scale. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Images like the sands of the Ganges appear across Mahayana sutras, and teachers use them to point past ordinary measuring; in this section the image serves to honor keeping and sharing the teaching.

original.note: Sanskrit: the Ganges; the sutra measures the immeasurable by its sand.

trapdoor: what you thought: a big number, to impress.
what it means: the treasure keeps growing beyond counting, and a few lines of understanding passed on still outweigh it.
what a scholar hears: the sutra repeats its comparison from section eight at a vastly larger scale; repetition with rising stakes is one of its ways of teaching.

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text.
All wording paraphrased (quoted: null). The sutra's 'three thousand great thousand worlds' and 'seven treasures' are left as 'worlds' and 'precious things' under the claims rule.
'Both are named, here and elsewhere in this sutra' (good man / good woman, shan nanzi shan nüren): confirm.
howItsDone says the Ganges-sands image appears across Mahayana sutras; it does in several (e.g. the Lotus Sutra), but a Keeper may prefer it narrowed to this sutra.
